title: The history of film editing
tagline: A century and more from a jammed camera in Paris to editing a Hollywood epic on a Mac.
intro: The first films were single shots. Within a few years, film-makers found that cutting between shots could leap across space and time, build suspense and even create feelings that were in no single shot. Machines like the Moviola and the flatbed made cutting precise, rebels like Godard broke the rules on purpose, and computers finally let editors change any cut in seconds.

eras.name: Discovering the cut
eras.summary: Film-makers learn that shots can be joined: close-ups, dissolves, action across cuts and cross-cutting for suspense.

eras.name: Montage
eras.summary: Soviet film-makers turn editing into a theory of meaning, while Hollywood gets its first editing machine.

eras.name: Invisible editing
eras.summary: Sound films and studio systems perfect continuity editing, cut on Moviolas and flatbed tables.

eras.name: Breaking the rules
eras.summary: New waves make cuts visible on purpose, and the first computer editors appear.

eras.name: The digital cutting room
eras.summary: Avid, Premiere, Final Cut and others replace film benches, and editing reaches every laptop and phone.

events.title: A camera jams, and a trick is born
events.text: Méliès said his camera jammed while filming a Paris street. When he projected the film, a bus seemed to turn into a hearse. He began stopping the camera and splicing film on purpose to make things appear and vanish.
events.why: It showed that film could be cut and joined to change what the audience believes they saw.

events.title: A close-up cut into a scene
events.text: In Grandma's Reading Glass, a boy looks through a magnifying glass, and Smith cuts to big circular close-ups of what he sees: a watch, a canary, his grandmother's eye.
events.why: It is one of the earliest films to cut between a wide shot and close-ups from a character's point of view.

events.title: A rescue that carries across the cuts
events.text: Fire! follows a fire from the street to a burning bedroom and back outside, across several shots. A firefighter carries a rescued person out of one shot and into the next.
events.why: It showed how action can carry on across a cut, the seed of continuity editing.

events.title: Dissolves join the scenes
events.text: A Trip to the Moon links its scenes with dissolves, one picture melting into the next, as its scientists fly to the Moon and back.
events.why: It made the dissolve part of cinema's grammar long before editing machines existed.

events.title: The Great Train Robbery
events.who: Edwin S. Porter, Edison Manufacturing Company
events.text: Porter's 12-minute western tells its story in about 14 shots, cutting between the robbers, the train and the telegraph office. It was a huge hit in the new nickelodeon theatres.
events.why: Cutting between places that are far apart helped audiences learn to follow a story told in separate shots.

events.title: Cross-cutting builds suspense
events.text: In The Lonely Villa, robbers break into a house while the father races home. Griffith cuts back and forth between them, faster and faster, until the rescue.
events.why: Cross-cutting between two lines of action became one of the most powerful tools for suspense.

events.title: Four stories, 2,500 years apart
events.text: Intolerance cuts between four stories set in ancient Babylon, the time of Jesus, 16th-century France and modern America, building all four towards their climaxes together.
events.why: It pushed cross-cutting further than anyone before and deeply influenced Soviet film-makers.

events.title: The Kuleshov experiment
events.who: Lev Kuleshov, with actor Ivan Mosjoukine
events.text: Kuleshov is said to have cut the same expressionless close-up next to shots of a bowl of soup, a girl in a coffin and a woman on a divan. As Pudovkin told it, viewers praised the actor's hunger, grief and desire. No footage survives.
events.why: It suggested that meaning comes from how shots are joined, not only from what is in them. Modern studies find a real but modest effect.

events.title: The Moviola
events.text: Serrurier turned his home movie projector into an upright editing machine with a small viewer. The first one went to Douglas Fairbanks's studio.
events.why: Editors could now watch film at any speed and find the exact frame to cut. Moviolas stayed the Hollywood standard until the 1970s.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin and the Odessa Steps
events.text: Eisenstein's film about a 1905 naval mutiny cuts together hundreds of short shots. In the Odessa Steps sequence, soldiers march down a long flight of steps into a fleeing crowd, and the editing stretches a few moments of terror into minutes.
events.why: It became the most studied example of montage: meaning and emotion made by shots colliding.

events.title: A film made only from old footage
events.text: Shub searched archives for old newsreels and home movies of the Russian royal family and edited them into The Fall of the Romanov Dynasty.
events.why: She showed that an editor can create a new story from footage shot by others, the root of the compilation documentary.

events.title: Man with a Movie Camera
events.who: Dziga Vertov and editor Elizaveta Svilova
events.text: A city symphony with no story and no actors, built from thousands of shots, with fast cutting, split screens and freeze frames. Svilova, the editor, even appears in the film at her editing bench.
events.why: It shows off almost every editing trick of the silent era in one film.

events.title: Flatbed editing tables
events.text: German companies built editing tables that lay the film flat on spinning plates, with a screen and separate picture and sound tracks. They came into wide use in the United States in the 1970s.
events.why: Flatbeds made it easy to run picture and sound together, forwards and back, and became the classic editing bench.

events.title: An editor who became a great director
events.text: Mukherjee edited Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin, a landmark of Indian realist cinema, before going on to direct films such as Anand.
events.why: Indian cinema has long drawn directors from the editing room, where they learn how scenes really work.

events.title: Breathless and the jump cut
events.text: Godard's first feature cut chunks out of continuous shots, so the characters seem to jump forward in time. Mainstream editors had worked hard to hide such cuts.
events.why: It made the jump cut a deliberate style. Today it is everywhere, from music videos to vlogs.

events.title: A matchstick becomes a desert sunrise
events.who: Anne V. Coates, for David Lean
events.text: In Lawrence of Arabia, Lawrence blows out a match and the film cuts straight to the sun rising over the desert. Coates won the Academy Award for editing.
events.why: It became one of the most admired match cuts in film.

events.title: From a bone to a spacecraft
events.text: In 2001: A Space Odyssey, an early human throws a bone into the air, and a match cut turns it into a satellite in orbit, jumping millions of years in one frame.
events.why: It showed how a single match cut can carry a huge leap in time and meaning.

events.title: The first non-linear editor
events.text: The CMX 600 stored video on disk drives the size of washing machines, holding about half an hour of footage, and let editors jump to any shot instantly.
events.why: It was the first step towards editing on computers, where you can change any cut without re-splicing everything after it.

events.title: EditDroid
events.text: EditDroid used LaserDiscs and a computer to find shots quickly, with an early on-screen timeline. It was shown at the NAB trade show in 1984 but sold only a few systems.
events.why: Many of its ideas, like the timeline, returned in later digital editors.

events.title: Avid Media Composer
events.text: Avid showed its computer editing system in 1989. Editors could cut with digitised copies of the footage, then send a list of their decisions to finish the film.
events.why: Media Composer became the standard for feature films and TV, and it still is in many cutting rooms.

events.title: Renu Saluja's first National Award
events.text: Saluja, a Film and Television Institute of India graduate, won the National Film Award for editing for Parinda, then again for Dharavi, Sardar and Godmother. She also cut Jaane Bhi Do Yaaro and 1942: A Love Story.
events.why: She became one of Indian cinema's most respected editors when the job was mostly done by men. An editing award is now named after her.

events.title: Editing comes to the desktop
events.text: Adobe Premiere let people edit video on an ordinary Apple Macintosh computer. Today's Premiere Pro is used for everything from YouTube videos to feature films.
events.why: Editing software stopped being only for studios.

events.title: In the Blink of an Eye
events.text: Murch's short book on editing asks why cuts work at all, and sets out his Rule of Six: emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, eye-trace 7%, the screen's 2D plane 5% and 3D space 4%.
events.why: It is still one of the most read books on editing.

events.title: A digital edit wins the Oscar
events.text: Murch's edit of The English Patient, cut on an Avid, won the Academy Award for Best Film Editing.
events.why: It was the first digitally edited film to win that Oscar, and the switch from film benches to computers sped up.

events.title: Final Cut Pro
events.text: Apple released Final Cut Pro, an editor that ran on an ordinary Mac and cost far less than professional systems.
events.why: Film students and independent film-makers could now edit professionally at home.

events.title: Cold Mountain is cut on a Mac
events.text: Murch and his assistant edited 597,000 feet of film for Cold Mountain on Final Cut Pro, the first major Hollywood feature cut on it.
events.why: It proved that affordable desktop software could handle a big studio film.

events.title: A. Sreekar Prasad, editor in 17 languages
events.text: Prasad has won National Awards for editing many times since 1989 and has cut films in 17 languages, from Dil Chahta Hai and Kannathil Muthamittal to RRR (2022).
events.why: His career shows how one editor can shape films across India's many languages.

series.title: How long a shot lasts in popular films
series.caption: Average shot duration in English-language popular films, by period, from James Cutting's 2016 study. Films now cut more than twice as often as in the early sound era.

facts: In Kuleshov's experiment the actor's face was the same shot every time, yet viewers said he looked hungry, sad or loving.
Walter Murch's Rule of Six ranks emotion at 51%, far above keeping the 180-degree line, which gets just 5%.
Cold Mountain's editors worked through 597,000 feet of film, about 110 hours of footage at 24 frames a second.
At the pace of films from 1990 to 2015, about 4.3 seconds a shot, a two-hour film holds around 1,700 shots.
